15. What is proved, what is trusted

Sooner or later someone will ask you what exactly they're trusting when they see a ✅, and they deserve a straight answer. A proof is only as good as what it is about. Every ✅ in this tour is a theorem about the Lean model Rel. Between your Ibis code and the model, and between the model and the engine, there is code that is not proved. Here is the honest picture:

data.text/markdown:
Proved (green): everything about Rel: the meaning of every operator, type safety, the rewrites, the abstract interpreter behind contracts, keys and relations between columns, window functions and tie-breaking, the absence of runtime errors, composition of contracts, the incremental update plans and their weight-column encoding, and the chain rule for views over views. Lean checks these mechanically, and #print axioms in SubstraitLean/Examples.lean confirms no step was skipped: the proofs use only Lean's three standard axioms. Trusted, guarded by tests:
  • the JSON parser and writer (do they translate plans faithfully?) and the rewrites the parser does on the way in (IN lists, COALESCE, RIGHT JOIN, …), guarded by golden tests and round trips;
  • the column descriptions taken from table schemas;
  • when DataFusion evaluates an expression (lazy CASE, eager AND, merged filters), which the runtime-error analysis relies on;
  • the sverify glue: change tables, consolidation, merging;
  • Delta and Iceberg: that a change feed turns the old snapshot into the new one, that writers enforce nullability and constraints, and that file statistics are correct (each refresh report names what it trusted);
  • the Polars translator, the SQL generator, and each engine itself.
The randomized tests compare the engines with each other and with Lean's Rel.eval, compare incremental views with full recomputation, check that proved postconditions hold on random data, and check that engines only ever fail where an error was reported. They have caught real engine bugs: an early version found DuckDB's Substrait reader running UNION ALL as UNION DISTINCT, which is why DuckDB now runs generated SQL instead. This is the normal shape of verified systems: a small proved core, plus a clearly labelled trusted boundary that is tested hard.

What the model doesn't cover yet

  • framed window aggregates (running totals, moving averages), ranks and NTILE;
  • incremental maintenance of aggregates, left, semi and anti joins, DISTINCT, LIMIT and windows (a node recomputes those and diffs the result);
  • relations needing more than "column plus constant", string contents, DECIMAL columns, counts across rows;
  • completeness: contracts say what every output row satisfies, not that no row is lost. The converse is a Lean theorem per plan today (IoT.window_complete in SubstraitLean/Completeness.lean), not something the checker reports.

data.text/html:
• Plan / relation (Rel): a tree of operators: Read, Filter, Project, Emit, Join, …
  • Semantics (Rel.eval): the reference interpreter that defines what a plan means.
  • Theorem: a statement quantified over all inputs, checked by Lean.
  • Hypothesis: a condition a theorem needs (e.g. "the filter only reads old columns").
  • Well-formed (Rel.WF): every column reference exists and union inputs agree on width.
  • Precondition / postcondition: what a transformation assumes about its inputs / guarantees about its output.
  • Abstract interpretation: running a plan on descriptions of values (can it be NULL? which values?) instead of values.
  • Key: columns no two rows agree on (sv.unique).
  • Deterministic: no ties in a window's order, so the engine has no choices to make.
  • Hoare triple {P} f {Q}: if P holds before f, Q holds after.
  • Bag: a table where duplicate rows count; order doesn't matter.
  • Z-set: a bag where rows carry integer weights; negative means deleted.
  • Delta (Δ): the change to a table, or to a query result.
  • Linear operator: one that handles each row independently, so Q(A + ΔA) = Q(A) + Q(ΔA).
  • Perm: "same rows, possibly in a different order."
  • Trusted base: the parts not covered by proofs.

A good first exercise in Lean: in Rewrites.lean, try to prove filter_project_pushdown without the hypothesis hp. Lean gets stuck exactly where a filter reads a column that only exists after the projection.
